A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TraceGrad research. The complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v4 reports original TraceGrad experiments across eight databases, component ablations, inference timings and DFT acceleration results.

after.justification: v5 retains these original results and adds gated alternatives, doubled-depth controls and combined inference-plus-DFT wall-time measurements.

M1.justification: Trace supervision, Clebsch-Gordan invariant encoding, gradient-induced equivariant features, residual combination and jointly weighted losses remain unchanged. Replacing generic target notation Q with Hamiltonian notation H does not change the procedure. New gated and doubled-depth models are experimental comparators.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same six DeepH crystalline databases and two QH9 molecular databases, retaining thermal-motion, twisted-bilayer, size-extrapolation and trajectory-generalization scenarios. The DFT experiments retain the same 50-molecule evaluation set; new controls and timing measurements do not expand data or task coverage.

E2.justification: v5 substantially expands the evaluated alternatives: DeepH-E3+Gate and DeepH-E3+TraceGate join the six-database comparisons in Tables 5–6, while DeepH-E3×2 and QHNet×2 provide doubled-depth comparisons in Table 7. Existing DeepH-E3, QHNet, HarmoSE and DeepH-2 comparisons are retained.

E3.justification: v5 adds controlled gradient-to-gate substitutions, doubled-depth models trained from scratch to convergence, and separate DFT-only, inference-only and combined-runtime metrics measured on one CPU thread. These extend evaluation within retained benchmarks; existing splits, sample counts and main accuracy metrics remain unchanged. Newly stated training limits do not establish changed budgets.

E4.justification: Appendix H newly tests gradients against gating, with and without trace supervision. Appendix J tests whether simply increasing backbone depth explains the accuracy gains, and Appendix K examines whether DFT savings survive inference overhead. These substantially strengthen mechanism and efficiency analyses beyond v4's retained component ablations and standalone timings.

E5.justification: v5 omits v4 Appendix I's statement that every GPU timing sample is inferred 50 times. Ten-run accuracy averages, fixed-seed descriptions and standard-deviation bounds remain, with their scope clarified per reported Hamiltonian MAE result. The new wall-time table reuses the existing convention of reporting means and standard deviations across 50 molecules.

E6.justification: Main accuracy scores, original ablation rows, DFT iteration ratios and HarmoSE results are unchanged. Added gated, doubled-depth and CPU timing results substantially expand the evidence. For example, v5 Table 5 reports MoS2 MAE of 0.346 meV for DeepH-E3+TraceGate versus 0.285 for TraceGrad; Table 9 reports QS combined runtime of 48.604 seconds for QHNet versus 41.941 for QHNet+TraceGrad.

T1.justification: The two core invariance/equivariance theorems and their proofs are retained with notation changes and relocation. v5 adds formal background definitions, including irreducible representations and Clebsch-Gordan decomposition, and a Kohn-Sham/eigenproblem formulation. Appendix I extends the complexity discussion to sparse downstream eigensolutions; it does not introduce a new core equivariance proof.

C1.justification: v5 frames the contribution more specifically around Hamiltonian prediction, whereas v4 foregrounded a general representation-learning framework with this application. It newly claims physical dimensional consistency between learned features and targets. The principal strict-equivariance, prediction-accuracy, downstream-property and DFT-acceleration claims remain.

C2.justification: Remark 4.3 introduces physical-dimensional correspondence as an explanation for preferring gradients to gating. New discussions interpret depth controls and combined timings as evidence of expressiveness and net computational savings. v4's broad future applications to other groups and nonphysical domains, and its interpretability caution in the ethics statement, are removed.

D1.justification: v5 explicitly states training limits of 5,000 epochs for the DeepH series and 300,000/260,000 steps for QS/QD. It also specifies single-task timing conditions and the single-thread Xeon Gold 6330 CPU environment. These improve documentation without establishing reruns of retained experiments; software versions, network dimensions, optimizers and backbone access links remain.

R1.justification: v5 cites Weiler et al. for gating and revises its critique around invariant supervision and dimensional coupling. It adds supporting group-theory, DFT and numerical-computation references, while removing Gu et al., Musaelian et al. and the autonomous-driving survey. The principal research context remains; HarmoSE's publication update represents the same cited work.

P1.justification: The title, abstract and introduction are substantially reframed around Hamiltonian prediction. Problem formalization moves to Appendix C, Section 3 becomes a preliminary-reading guide, and a new appendix-summary section is added. Background and implementation sections are reorganized, complexity and timing discussions are separated, and the ethics and future-work sections disappear.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from single-column to two-column layout. Figure 2 is redrawn to show multiple atomic-pair Hamiltonian matrices, ablation tables gain gated rows, and new cost/accuracy and CPU wall-time tables are introduced. The DFT-ratio table moves into the appendices. Figures 3–7 retain their visual content despite relocation and resizing.

improvement.justification: v5 strengthens the experimental case: Tables 5–7 address gating and increased depth as alternative explanations for accuracy gains, while Table 9 demonstrates DFT savings including inference costs, beyond v4's iteration ratios and separate GPU timings. Training-limit disclosure also helps reproducibility. These gains are tempered by the omitted GPU repetition count and the new dimensional-consistency claim, which the retained equivariance proofs do not establish.
